caption:
This morning: United banned outside AI agents from booking flights, while Southwest opened its inventory to ChatGPT. Two airlines, two opposite policies.

The data: Propellic is reported to say 57% of agent flight bookings go through an intermediary (NOT CONFIRMED: we could not find this figure on the cited Travel Daily News page). AI models went straight to airline sites only about 5% of the time (Bain). AI queries could hit 200,000 searches per booking (PhocusWire).

My take: drawing a line is the right start, but measure who is actually booking before you write the rule.

Comment CHECK and I will DM you what I find.

Sources in the first comment.

scenes: This morning I covered United banning outside AI agents from booking flights, while Southwest opened its inventory to ChatGPT. I went back in to check the numbers.
First, Propellic is said to have found 57% of agent flight bookings go through an intermediary, but we could not confirm that on the page cited.
Second, Bain tested three AI models on flight searches. They went directly to an airline website only about 5% of the time.
Third, PhocusWire's analysis says AI queries could reach 200,000 searches for every booking, which shows why airlines worry about cost.
Drawing a line is a start, but who is really booking? If you use these agents, what do you see? Comment CHECK and tell me.
